Article Title: Hockey World Cup: Netherlands wear blue on blue turf, India play in saffron after 'visibility' claim
Article Text:
India walked out in saffron. The Netherlands played in blue

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

For decades, blue has been the colour most closely linked with Indian sport. Across disciplines, Indian teams have worn blue while representing the country on the international stage. But ahead of the FIH Hockey World Cup in the Netherlands and Belgium, Hockey India unveiled a new saffron jersey for both the men's and women's teams last month.The reason, according to Hockey India, was visibility . The federation said the "blue playing uniform tended to blend/merge with the blue synthetic playing surface, which is now the standard colour of international hockey pitches. This visual similarity affected on-field clarity and visibility for the players."However, in India women's first match of the second round of the FIH World Cup againt the co-hosts Netherlands on Friday in Amstelveen, India walked out in saffron, while the Netherlands played in blue. On the same blue turf where India had argued blue jerseys reduced visibility. Perhaps the Dutch did not have the same visibility concerns.The change in India's primary jersey colour drew criticism from former captains Pargat Singh, Dhanraj Pillay and Viren Rasquinha when it was announced last month.Pargat was the most direct in his criticism. "Everything in the country is being saffronised," said former India captain Pargat Singh while criticizing Hockey India's decision.Dhanraj, who played 339 international matches for India, including four Olympics, four World Cups and four Champions Trophy tournaments, questioned why a colour associated with Indian hockey for decades was replaced."The blue jersey has become the identity of Indian hockey. Being one of the colours of our national flag, saffron is important and auspicious but it has never been the traditional colour of Indian hockey. I don't understand why this has suddenly changed after so many years," Dhanraj was quoted as saying by news agency PTI.Pargat also warned against bringing politics into sport."Everything in the country is being saffronised – education, history and now sports too. This is worrying. Sports unite people and rise above religion, caste and politics. It is unfortunate if such thinking enters sports as well," he had said after Hockey India's decision, as quoted by PTI.Meanwhile, in the match on Friday, Indian women's hockey team produced a disciplined defensive performance against the hosts. Veteran goalkeeper Savita led the backline as India restricted the world No. 1 side and three-time defending champions for long periods.The Netherlands eventually won 2-0 in the first match of the second round at the packed Wagner Stadium. Both goals came from penalty corners, while India did not concede a field goal.The Indian goalkeepers and defenders, who had saved 12 penalty corners in the previous match against England, prevented the world No. 1 team from playing freely at the packed Wagner Stadium, and the co-hosts could not score a single field goal.
Article Summary: India walked out in saffron, while the Netherlands played in blue. The change in India's primary jersey colour drew criticism from former captains Pargat Singh, Dhanraj Pillay and Viren Rasquinha. The Netherlands eventually won 2-0 in the first match of the second round at the packed Wagner Stadium.

Article Title: Mitchell Starc unleashes havoc as Australia bowl Bangladesh out for 64 after Darwin disaster
Article Text:
Mitchell Starc

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Australia bounced back from their nine-wicket defeat in the first Test at Darwin by bowling Bangladesh out for just 64 on the first day of the second and final Test in Mackay on Saturday.After winning the toss, Australia captain Pat Cummins chose to bowl first, and Mitchell Starc made an immediate impact. The left-arm fast bowler finished with 6/12 after completing the sixth-fastest five-wicket haul in Test cricket.Bangladesh were in trouble within the first session. Starc took five wickets in the first 45 minutes as the visitors slipped to 12/5 before reaching lunch at 35/6.Starc struck with the first ball of the match, dismissing opener Shadman Islam. The delivery moved in before leaving the left-hander, who edged it to Cameron Green at gully.It was the fourth time Starc has taken a wicket with the first ball of a Test innings, after dismissing Dimuth Karunaratne, Rory Burns and Yashasvi Jaiswal in previous matches. It was also the ninth time he had taken a wicket in the first over of a Test.Shadman became only the second Bangladesh opener to be dismissed off the first ball of a Test innings after Hannan Sarkar, who suffered the same fate three times against West Indies fast bowler Pedro Collins, as per Cricinfo.Starc picked up his second wicket in his next over when Tanzid Hasan guided the first ball to Beau Webster at second slip. Tanzid, who scored a century in the previous Test, registered his second consecutive duck after that innings.Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto was trapped lbw with the very next ball. He reviewed the decision, but it stayed with Starc on umpire's call.Starc missed out on a hat-trick, but Mominul Haque soon became his fourth wicket after edging a wide delivery to Green at gully.The fifth wicket came in Starc's next over when Litton Das was given out lbw for a duck. Webster had dropped Litton off the previous delivery before Kumar Dharmasena raised his finger. TV umpire Richard Illingworth confirmed the decision after the review.Bangladesh's score of 12/5 became their lowest total after losing five wickets in a Test innings.Mushfiqur Rahim and Mehidy Hasan Miraz then resisted for the next 10 overs, mostly through defensive batting, before Cummins broke the stand by bowling Mushfiqur for five.Cummins also dismissed Mehidy Hasan Miraz for 11 after he was caught in the slips and later had Taskin Ahmed caught at square leg for one.Josh Hazlewood added the wicket of Hasan Mahmud for 10.Bangladesh's lower order managed to take the total past 50 after the top order collapsed. Starc returned to end the innings by having Shoriful Islam caught behind for 14, wrapping up Bangladesh's innings for 64.
Article Summary: Mitchell Starc takes five wickets in first 45 minutes as Bangladesh slip to 12/5. Australia captain Pat Cummins chooses to bowl first after winning toss. Left-arm fast bowler finished with 6/12 after completing sixth-fastest five- wicket haul in Test cricket.

Article Title: ‘Blown away and hammered’: Ex-England captain says Pakistan lack ‘spirit’ after embarrassing defeat
Article Text:
Pakistan's Ali Usman is struck on the shoulder from the bowling of England's Jofra Archer

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former England captain Michael Vaughan has expressed serious concern over Pakistan’s current Test side after their comprehensive defeat against England at Headingley, saying he had rarely seen them look so short of confidence and fight.England needed less than three days to complete an innings-and-103-run victory in the opening Test, taking a 1-0 lead in the three-match series. Pakistan were dismissed for 171 in their first innings and then folded for 135 in the second, spending just 85.4 overs at the crease across the match.Vaughan was particularly troubled by the manner of Pakistan’s capitulation rather than simply the margin of defeat. Speaking on BBC Test Match Special, he said: “They've been absolutely blown away. They've been hammered. I've never seen them look so timid.”He also questioned Pakistan’s overall performance, pointing to shortcomings in their tactics and the difference in quality between the two sides.“The tactical side wasn't there. The skill level and the class between the sides, Pakistan look a long way short,” Vaughan said. “I hope they can find something over the next couple of days. They'll get criticised, and rightly so; hopefully, that will force them to find something.”England’s dominance was built around a disciplined pace attack and a strong batting effort. Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue claimed five wickets each in Pakistan’s first innings, while Jofra Archer struck early in the second innings before Robinson and Tongue returned to dismantle the lower order.Both Robinson and Tongue finished with eight wickets in the match. Robinson was named Player of the Match after figures of 8/80, while Tongue took 8/89.England’s batters had earlier put the hosts in complete control after they posted 409, securing a 238-run lead. Harry Brook scored 91, Jordan Cox made 73, Joe Root contributed 66 and Dan Lawrence added 51.For Vaughan, Pakistan’s decline in intensity was especially disappointing given the aggressive identity traditionally associated with their cricket.“I look at this side and feel quite sad watching them this week,” he said. “I've seen many Pakistan sides play, and this side just seem to be lacking all that spirit and fight we've come accustomed to seeing.”The defeat also marked the beginning of a new era for England under returning captain Root following the retirement of Ben Stokes and Brendon McCullum ’s departure as Test coach.Pakistan will now have several days to regroup before the second Test at Lord’s begins on Thursday. England, meanwhile, will look to carry their momentum into the next match as they attempt to extend their series advantage.
Article Summary: England beat Pakistan by an innings and 103 runs in the opening Test. Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue claimed five wickets each in Pakistan’s first innings. Jofra Archer struck early in the second innings before Robinson and Tongue returned to dismantle the lower order.

Article Title: From football dream to hockey hero: Bichu Devi’s journey to India’s No. 1 goalkeeper
Article Text:
(From left) Bichu Devi Kharibam with Pirmin Blaak and Savita​

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bichu Devi Kharibam never planned to play hockey. Goalkeeping was even further from her thoughts. She had gone to SAI Imphal with one ambition — to make it as a footballer. But arriving two days late for the trials meant the selections were complete and there were no places left.Then came a suggestion that would change the course of her sporting career. The director, who knew Bichu’s family, suggested she try hockey.“I didn’t want to play hockey at all. I cried and told my father that I wanted to continue with football,” she recalled in an interview with TOI.Her father, however, persuaded her to give hockey two months and then decide. She gradually began to enjoy the sport, particularly after she started scoring goals as a striker.Goalkeeping was still nowhere on her radar until an Olympian coach noticed her height and physical attributes and suggested that she could make a good goalkeeper.“I didn’t understand much at that time. Playing for India wasn’t even in my thoughts,” said the player from Manipur.Yet, almost against her wishes, Bichu found herself in goal, making her debut as a goalkeeper at the sub-junior nationals in Ranchi in 2015.She played well and that performance set her on a path that would eventually take her to one of the biggest nights of her career more than a decade later at Wagener Stadium in Amstelveen.With the World Cup second round at stake, England pushed hard in the closing stages, but the Indian goalkeeper stood firm. And when the decisive moment arrived, Bichu produced a last-gasp save that preserved India’s draw and sent them into the second round.For someone who had once cried because she didn’t want to play hockey, it was a moment to cherish. But perhaps the signs that Bichu could become a special goalkeeper had been there from the beginning.Vandana, a coach at the Madhya Pradesh Hockey Academy, first saw Bichu at the 2015 Ranchi nationals. “She was good, energetic and a beginner at that time,” Vandana recalled.It was there that the then Manipur coach approached Vandana and asked if Bichu could join MP Academy. There was no looking back after that. A week later, Bichu travelled with Vandana to Gwalior for the academy trials and was selected.What stood out was her athleticism.“As a goalkeeper, you are already wearing a lot of equipment, so you have the weight of your body as well as the goalkeeper’s kit. You have to fall down and get back up quickly. You have to be very fast and agile, and she was really good at that,” Vandana said.Her fitness was another advantage. “Her lean muscle mass also helped her, as did her height,” Vandana said.The sport she had originally wanted to play also played a big role in her development.“Playing football helped me a lot with kicking, diving, getting back on my feet quickly and directing the ball into safe areas. Because of my football background, I already understood many of those movements, so I didn’t have to spend extra time learning them after becoming a goalkeeper,” Bichu said. “I could focus on learning goalkeeping-specific things like positioning and body shape.”Her development was also helped by someone who knew exactly what it took to be India’s No. 1.Savita Punia had first seen Bichu when she was still playing for the junior team and immediately felt she had the qualities of a good goalkeeper. Years later, as Bichu grew into the senior side, that belief only strengthened.For Savita, one of Bichu’s biggest strengths is not simply her athletic ability but her attitude towards learning. “She is very sincere about learning and improving. There are very few players who approach their work with that level of sincerity. Bichu is one of them. She works with a lot of dedication,” she said.This mentor-student relationship between the two goalkeepers has only grown stronger over the years. And when Bichu made that last-minute save on Thursday night, Savita, watching from the sidelines, was among the first to celebrate, jumping with joy as India secured their place in the second round.While it’s impossible to predict what lies ahead for India in this World Cup, one thing is becoming increasingly clear — the goalkeeper who never planned to play hockey could be India’s No. 1 for years to come.
Article Summary: Bichu Devi Kharibam never planned to play hockey. The goalkeeper made her debut as a goalkeeper at the sub-junior nationals in Ranchi in 2015. Her performance set her on a path that would eventually take her to one of the biggest nights of her career more than a decade later.

Article Title: Jamal Musiala to miss Bayern’s Supercup opener as club reveals shocking cause behind recent collapses
Article Text:
Jamal Musiala collapses again during Bayern match, reveals diagnosis and reassures fans he remains optimistic/ Image: X

Musiala ruled out of Bayern's first trophy match

The Athletic

Medication change linked to the two episodes

What happened to Musiala?

Jamal Musiala collapsed mid-game shortly after scoring, with extreme heat reportedly linked to dizziness and circulatory problems/ Image:X

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bayern take no chances with their key player

Bayern Munich will be without Jamal Musiala for Saturday’s German Supercup against Borussia Dortmund, with the club choosing not to rush the midfielder back after he collapsed during two successive pre-season matches.The decision comes after Musiala revealed earlier this week that he had been diagnosed with “temporary, brief, but easily treatable absence seizures” caused by a neurological dysfunction. Bayern have since explained that the episodes became visible following a change in his medication, and the club is now adjusting his treatment.According to, Bayern have confirmed that Musiala will not be included in the squad for Saturday’s Supercup.Head coach Vincent Kompany said the 23-year-old has been training individually this week as the club works with medical experts and adjusts his treatment.“It’s the first time for the public, so obviously a lot of questions arise,” Kompany said. “We’ve been dealing with it for longer, though. That initial shock was a while ago, since then we’ve been given a lot more information and have made decisions with the help of the best experts.”Kompany added that Musiala has the full support of the club and that Bayern are optimistic about his situation.“Jamal has the support of everyone. Internally we’re at a point where we’re not speaking about it much anymore. We’ve been prepared for it for a long time, have our processes and are very optimistic,” he said.Bayern board member for sport Max Eberl explained that Musiala's two recent collapses occurred after a change to his medication.“He changed something in the medication, which is why the episodes became visible,” Eberl said. “Now we want to get back to where it was before, when these episodes didn’t occur.”“He’s made a huge step forward in his football. He’s showing it in training too. We’re looking forward to when he can show that in matches again. He’s not in the squad for tomorrow. It’s about adapting to the treatment.”Musiala collapsed during Bayern's friendly against RB Leipzig on Saturday after appearing dazed and losing his balance. He was helped safely to the ground by teammates before being attended to by the medical staff.Four days later, he suffered another episode during the friendly against Heidenheim, collapsing just minutes after coming on as a substitute. On both occasions, Bayern's medical staff immediately attended to him while players from both teams helped shield him from view.Musiala was able to leave the pitch on his own on both occasions, although he appeared disoriented.Following the Heidenheim incident, Musiala explained his diagnosis on Instagram.“I’ve been diagnosed with temporary, brief, but easily treatable absence seizures, which are due to a neurological dysfunction,” he wrote.“These can lead to the recent incidents, like the one against Leipzig or now in Heidenheim.”Musiala also sought to reassure supporters about his condition, writing: “I know these things might seem scary at first glance — but for me, they’re currently part of my everyday life. I’m receiving the best medical treatment and am very optimistic. Importantly, there is no further health risk. I have a very good feeling and am on the right track.”Eberl said Musiala himself wanted to explain the situation publicly.“It was Jamal’s wish to communicate it,” Eberl said. “Internally we’ve known about it for longer, including the players. For us it’s become everyday life.”Musiala remains one of Bayern's most important players, with Transfermarkt valuing the 23-year-old at €100 million.His absence is therefore significant as Bayern prepare for their first opportunity to win silverware of the new season. The Supercup brings together last season's Bundesliga champions Bayern and runners-up Dortmund.Bayern won the Bundesliga for a second consecutive season, while Dortmund finished second.For now, however, Musiala's return to competitive action will wait. Bayern's immediate priority is getting his treatment back to the point where the recent episodes no longer occur before considering his return to matches.
Article Summary: Bayern Munich midfielder Jamal Musiala has been ruled out of Saturday's German Supercup against Borussia Dortmund. The 23-year-old suffered two collapses during pre-season matches against RB Leipzig and Heidenheim. He revealed earlier this week that he had been diagnosed with “temporary, brief, but easily treatable absence seizures” caused by a neurological dysfunction. Bayern have explained that the episodes became visible following a change in his medication, and the club is now adjusting his treatment.

Article Title: Ancy Sojan: Thrissur girl who broke 22-year-old record, now aiming for Asiad gold
Article Text:
Kerala's Ancy Sojan (PTI Photo)

Forged in sand

Backwater bounty

Kerala vs Karnataka: Record rivalry

Kerala vs Karnataka

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

New Delhi: Ancy Sojan was around three when Anju Bobby George launched herself into the air at the end of a brisk run-up in Athens and set a seemingly unsurpassable national long-jump record. For much of the two decades that followed, Ancy may not have spent a lot of time thinking about George’s record, because her sights were set elsewhere, on the athletics track — remarkable for someone who would eventually overhaul the mark that had stood for 22 years.Now, the girl from Thrissur in central Kerala is looking to write the next chapter in the story at next month’s Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. She’ll get to warm up for Japan at two events in India. The first of those comes next week in Bhubaneswar, the city where she jumped 6.88m in June to better George’s 6.83m set in 2004.Gearing up for another stab at international glory — she had won the long-jump silver at the last Asian Games — if the 25-year-old gets a moment to reflect on her journey, she would undoubtedly find herself back on the vast shoreline of Nattika, the unlikely setting that put her on the path to becoming an elite athlete.Ancy’s father, an autorickshaw driver, used to bring his daughter to the beach in Nattika, where she would sprint on the loose sands, dreaming of becoming a sprinter. But destiny had other plans.“Unknowingly, Ancy was putting herself through nature’s own strength training programme. Running on that loose sand builds strength in the calves and ankles,” said P Ramachandran, the sprinter from Nattika who competed in the 2000 Sydney Olympics 4x400m relay.Ancy’s coach, Anoop Joseph, echoes the thought.“Running on the uneven surface of the sand forces your ankles, feet and core to stabilise your body. It can help maintain control during approach and takeoff,” he explains.Ancy made the switch to long jump around 2015, when she won bronze with a 4.93m jump at the U-14 state school games. Then, in 2019, she burst onto the Indian athletics scene with a 6.26m jump at the National School Athletics meet in Sangrur, Punjab.Sanoj VV, her childhood coach who played a pivotal role in Ancy’s transition from a sprinter to a long jumper, remembers the spark he had seen then.“Back then I had predicted that Ancy would break George’s national record. People laughed at me. Today my prediction has come true,” he said, adding that “it was remarkable considering she was so tiny back then”.Following her feat in Bhubaneswar, accolades have poured in for Ancy from several quarters, including a congratulatory call from Kerala chief minister V D Satheeshan.When asked about his ward’s 6.88m leap, Anoop, however, chose to downplay it.“Technically, it was a perfect jump. But let’s not get carried away. We’re still working on her motor qualities, speed and strength,” he said.Anoop has a point. Records in women’s long jump tend to have surprising longevity. The world record, of 7.52m, was set by erstwhile USSR’s Galina Chistyakova in 1988, the same year that the US’ Jackie Joyner-Kersee set the Olympic record of 7.4m at Seoul.Ancy had won her Asian Games silver with a jump of 6.63m, much below her best. The gold in the last edition, held in China, was bagged by the host country’s Xiong Shiqi with a 6.73m jump.For Ancy, the run-up to Japan — apart from the World Athletics Continental Tour in Bhubaneswar, which begins on August 22, she’ll also take part in the Indian Athletics Series in Delhi from September 10 — comes against the backdrop of a personal worry.“My father is recovering from an injury, and his mobility remains restricted. He has not resumed driving his autorickshaw. It remains a concern,” she told TOI.A fishing hamlet known for its frequent dolphin sightings, Nattika is also part of cinema lore as the backdrop for the timeless, National Award-winning Malayalam film ‘Chemmeen’. Part of its claim to fame is also the raft of Olympians and international athletes that it has given India.Apart from Ramachandran, Nattika has produced Anjali P D, a track athlete, and discus thrower Athulya P. Volleyball also has a good following in this sports-loving village.“But no one from Nattika has managed to capture the national imagination like Ancy,” Ramachandran said.Yet, the village lacks a Sports Authority of India centre and is still waiting for a 400m synthetic track for budding athletes.“Aspiring athletes from Nattika have to travel to Kunnamkulam or the SAI centre in Palakkad, which typically takes at least two hours of travel by road,” Ramachandran said.In recent years, Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president P T Usha has been campaigning for a synthetic track at the Corporation Stadium in Thrissur.“The progress has been slow,” said Sanoj VV.Sanoj had trained his ward till she was 18 at a ramshackle sand pit on the fringes of the National Fisheries Higher Secondary School in Nattika.“We created a makeshift sand pit for Ancy’s training back then,” he said. “Last year, the government inaugurated a modest 200-metre synthetic track here.”The progression of the national women’s long-jump record has been a two-way battle between Karnataka and Kerala. The elite list features no more than seven athletes who’ve held the record since Karnataka’s Angel Mary Joseph became the first Indian to breach the 6m mark in 1978.Till Ancy Sojan set the new mark of 6.88m in Bhubaneswar in June this year, the honours were evenly split between the two southern states.Mercy Mathew, who held the record in the early 1980s, says she was surprised that Anju Bobby George’s stay at the top lasted 22 years.Talking about Ancy, she feels the girl from Thrissur is capable of bigger leaps.“I wonder why it took this long (for George’s record to be broken), though there were quite a few who looked capable of breaking her mark,” she said. “Those were the days when we knew nothing about records. My first national record came at the inter-university meet in February 1980 in Pune,” she recalled.Mercy said Ancy is capable of adding another 10-12cm to the new record.“I’ve seen her progress from the days when she competed at the school games. She is an aggressive athlete and is capable of giving her best under pressure,” Mercy, who runs her own athletics academy in Kochi, told TOI.Mercy’s best of 6.26m came at the 1982 Asian Games, where she won silver.George’s era began with a record-breaking 6.37m on August 3, 1999, and she then took charge of the record book, improving her mark before producing her personal best of 6.83m in the 2004 Olympics final.
Article Summary: Ancy Sojan won the long-jump silver at the last Asian Games. She jumped 6.88m in June to better Anju Bobby George’s 6.83m set in 2004. The 25-year-old is looking to write the next chapter in the story at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games next month.

Article Title: Lakshya Sen suffers stunning upset, but Ayush Shetty and PV Sindhu march on
Article Text:
India's PV Sindhu (ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

New Delhi: A stunned silence swept across the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium as India’s premier men’s singles hope, Lakshya Sen, cracked under the weight of expectations. In a major upset at the BWF World Championships 2026, the world No. 14 shuttler crashed out in the second round, humbled 19-21, 21-19, 21-17 by USA’s unheralded Garret Tan, ranked 92nd, in a gruelling 73-minute contest.Lakshya’s display on Wednesday was alarmingly inconsistent, plagued by baffling errors in judgement. While Tan grappled with the drift, Lakshya appeared perpetually unsettled.Much like his sluggish opening-round encounter, Lakshya started at a pedestrian pace, searching fruitlessly for timing while the American settled quickly. The Indian did manage to summon a fleeting burst of resolve midway through the opening game, rattling off late points to erase a deficit, level the score and snatch the opener 21-19.Yet, any expectations that the opening-game heist would settle Lakshya’s nerves were swiftly extinguished.The ensuing two games exposed glaring tactical vulnerabilities. Missing routine shots proved to be Lakshya’s bane. Even as he scrapped to stay within touching distance in the second game, Tan held firm in the clutch moments to edge it 21-19 and draw level.The decider laid bare Lakshya’s unravelling. A barrage of unforced errors leaked from his racquet. The contest took a dramatic turn when Tan began suffering from severe cramps midway through the third game.Writhing in pain between points, it momentarily seemed the American might be forced to retire. Yet, rather than pouncing on a physically compromised opponent, Lakshya remained hesitant and flat-footed. Showing remarkable courage, Tan soldiered through to keep his nose in front.Though Lakshya attempted a frantic late fightback, the gap was simply too wide to bridge.“I would give a lot of credit to my opponent; he played a very solid game. I think I gave it my all in the end, but it was just not enough to win this match,” Lakshya said.While Lakshya’s shock exit cast a shadow over the home crowd, the 21-year-old sensation Ayush Shetty provided an electric lift. Shetty dismantled Sri Lanka’s Duminda Abeywickrama 21-8, 21-10 in a breathless 26-minute masterclass to cruise into the pre-quarterfinals.Two-time Olympic medallist PV Sindhu also advanced to the pre-quarters, subduing Canada’s Wen Yu Zhang 21-16, 21-17 in 35 minutes. Although Zhang staged a brief fightback to draw level in the second game, Sindhu shifted gears midway to pull away for a straight-games victory.However, there was heartbreak for 18-year-old Unnati Hooda in the women’s singles draw. The teenager pushed Canada’s experienced 13th seed Michelle Li to the absolute limit across 58 minutes before narrowly bowing out 21-11, 9-21, 21-23.India’s mixed doubles pairing of Dhruv Kapila and Tanisha Crasto raced past Macau’s Leong Iok Chong and Ng Weng Chi 21-11, 21-11 in just 30 minutes to advance.The men’s doubles campaign suffered a setback as Arjun MR and Hariharan Amsakarunan lost 17-21, 14-21 to South Korea’s Kang Min Hyuk and Ki Dong Ju in 43 minutes.Satwik-Chirag duo gets walkoverIndia’s top-ranked men’s doubles pair of Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty moved into the pre-quarterfinals without hitting a shot after Scotland’s Alexander Dunn and Adam Pringle withdrew from their scheduled second-round clash here on Wednesday.
Article Summary: Lakshya Sen, India's premier men's singles hope, cracked under the weight of expectations. The world No. 14 shuttler crashed out in the second round, humbled by USA’s unheralded Garret Tan, ranked 92nd, in a gruelling 73-minute contest.

Article Title: After shocking Darwin defeat, Australia make big change for Bangladesh Test
Article Text:
Australian captain Pat Cummins, second left, leads his players from the field following their nine wicket loss to Bangladesh AP/PTI)

Australia's playing XI for the second Test is:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Australia have confirmed a key change at the top of their batting order for the second Test against Bangladesh, with recalled opener Matthew Renshaw set to make his return to the Test side in Mackay.Captain Pat Cummins confirmed in his pre-match press conference that Renshaw will open the innings after Australia made changes following their shock nine-wicket defeat in the series opener in Darwin.The second Test will mark Renshaw’s return to Test cricket after more than three years. The 30-year-old last played a Test in Delhi against India in 2023, when he appeared as a concussion substitute for regular opener David Warner.Since then, Renshaw has continued to represent Australia in ODI and T20I cricket, but his latest recall comes after Australia’s top order struggled badly in the opening Test against Bangladesh.Renshaw has replaced Jake Weatherald, who has been dropped after the defeat. Marnus Labuschagne and Beau Webster are expected to retain their places in the batting line-up.Australia also faced a major selection call over veteran spinner Nathan Lyon . Lyon managed only one wicket in the first Test, prompting discussion about whether Australia could go with an all-pace attack as they look to level the two-match series.However, Australia have ultimately decided to retain Lyon. The selectors confirmed his place in the XI shortly after Cummins addressed the media.Matthew Renshaw, Travis Head, Marnus Labuschagne, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey (wk), Beau Webster, Pat Cummins (c), Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood.The decision to retain Lyon is significant given Australia's recent willingness to rely entirely on pace in certain conditions. The team used an all-seam attack twice in pink-ball Tests last year.However, leaving Lyon out of a red-ball Test when fit would have been a major break from tradition. The last time Australia omitted the veteran spinner from a Test despite him being fit was 14 years ago, at the WACA Ground in 2012.Australia now face a must-win Test in Mackay after Bangladesh took a 1-0 lead in the series with their nine-wicket victory in Darwin. Renshaw's return at the top and Lyon's continued presence in the attack will be central to Australia's attempt to bounce back.
Article Summary: Matthew Renshaw set to make his return to the Test side in Mackay. The 30-year- old last played a Test in Delhi against India in 2023. Article Title: Treesa Jolly-Gayatri Gopichand end India’s 15-year wait, assure World Championships medal

An MRI subsequently revealed two high-grade muscle tears and two ligament tears, forcing her into a lengthy rehabilitation programme.The pair eventually began their comeback at the Indonesia Open before competing at the US Open. Article Title: 'Crowd was amazing': Treesa-Gayatri reveal how home crowd helped them stun world no. 4 pair
Article Text:
India's Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopich defeat China's Zhang Shuxian and Jia Yifan (ANI Photo)

Gopichand's advice makes the difference

'We just want to stay calm'

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Following in the footsteps of Jwala and Ashwini

Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand produced one of the biggest victories of their careers as they stunned world No. 4 Jia Yi Fan and Zhang Shu Xian to storm into the semifinals of the BWF World Championships and secure India's first medal at the ongoing edition. The Indian duo overcame a slow start to script a remarkable comeback, defeating the Chinese pair 16-21, 21-15, 21-13 in a thrilling 70-minute quarter-final at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium.The victory ended India's long wait for a medal in women's doubles at the World Championships. Treesa and Gayatri became only the second Indian women's doubles pair to win a Worlds medal, following Jwala Gutta and Ashwini Ponnappa , who claimed bronze in 2011.The home crowd played a crucial role in lifting the Indian pair during the tense encounter, with Treesa and Gayatri acknowledging the energy and support from the stands after their stunning victory."We're really happy that we converted this win into this semifinal and getting a medal, but it's not stopping yet. There are matches coming tomorrow also," Treesa told reporters after the win."And obviously, I want to thank, I think it's teamwork for us, everyone that helped us to achieve this, and really grateful, and obviously I want to thank the home crowd people. I think the crowd was amazing today; that was really giving positive vibes to us," she added.The Indian pair also revealed the advice they received from chief national coach and legendary former shuttler Pullela Gopichand during the tense battle. With the match slipping away after they lost the opening game, Gopichand urged the duo to remain composed and focus on the present moment."From the start, he was telling that be in the present moment and very calm, because that helped us score the points, and that really worked today," Treesa said."We were just be patient and waiting for the right time to score the points. I think that really worked," she added.Treesa and Gayatri had entered the quarter-final with a difficult record against Jia and Zhang, having lost all three of their previous meetings against the Chinese pair. They once again found themselves under pressure after dropping the opening game, but the Indians dramatically changed the momentum in the second game.Their composure under pressure eventually helped them complete a memorable comeback and book a place in the last four.The Indian duo will now face top seeds Liu Sheng Shu and Tan Ning of China in the semifinals. Gayatri said the pair will look to stick to the same approach that helped them overcome Jia and Zhang."It was a pretty tough match. We were down, trailing, and then even in the second set it was very tricky, but then we told each other to stay calm, and I think that's what we're going to do tomorrow as well," Gayatri said."We just want to stay calm, and we just want to get on court and give our 100 per cent, just enjoy as we did today," she added.Treesa and Gayatri also drew inspiration from Jwala Gutta and Ashwini Ponnappa, the first Indian women's doubles pair to win a World Championships medal."Yeah, 100%. I think they're one of the ideals for us. They have created history for India in women's doubles, and I always praise and admire them," Treesa said.
Article Summary: Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand beat world No. 4 Jia Yi Fan and Zhang Shu Xian 16-21 21-15 21-13. Victory ends India's long wait for a medal in women's doubles at the World Championships. Indian duo will now face top seeds Liu Sheng Shu and Tan Ning of China in the semifinals.

Article Title: Joe Root’s captaincy return begins in style as England crush Pakistan by innings and 103 runs in 1st Test
Article Text:
England crush Pakistan inside three days (Agency Image)

Robinson, Tongue trigger Pakistan collapse

Brook, Cox and Root power England ahead

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistan crumble again as England seal emphatic win

England made a stunning start to the new era under returning captain Joe Root, thrashing Pakistan by an innings and 103 runs inside three days in the first Test at Headingley, Leeds, on Friday.In their first Test since Ben Stokes' retirement and Brendon McCullum's departure as head coach, England produced a dominant all-round performance to take a 1-0 lead in the three-match series. After bowling Pakistan out for 171 in their first innings, England piled up 409 before dismissing the visitors for just 135 in their second innings.The victory was England's biggest innings win over Pakistan at Headingley and their second successive innings victory over the visitors at the venue, following their innings-and-55-run win in 2018.England won the toss and opted to bowl, and their decision paid immediate dividends as their pace attack dismantled Pakistan's batting order on the opening day. Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue shared all 10 wickets, claiming five apiece as Pakistan slipped from 117/3 to 171 all out. Abdullah Shafique offered the only substantial resistance with a patient 61, but the rest of the Pakistan batting line-up struggled against England's disciplined pace attack.England then ended the opening day strongly at 112/2, laying the foundation for a commanding first-innings lead.England's batters took complete control on the second day despite several rain interruptions. Harry Brook narrowly missed out on a century, scoring 91 off 93 balls, while Jordan Cox contributed a fluent 73. Root, back as England's Test captain following Stokes' retirement, scored 66, while Dan Lawrence added a brisk 51.Pakistan's left-arm spinner Ali Usman provided some relief for the visitors, claiming his maiden five-wicket haul in Test cricket with figures of 5/95. However, England continued to pile on the runs and eventually reached 409. England's total gave them a massive 238-run first-innings advantage and left Pakistan facing an uphill battle to save the Test.Pakistan's second innings followed a familiar pattern as their top order once again struggled against England's pace attack. The visitors reached lunch at 59/3, but a brief resistance from Mohammad Rizwan, who top-scored with 41, could not prevent another collapse.Jofra Archer and Robinson took charge of the attack as England wrapped up the Pakistan innings for 135 in just 37.3 overs. Archer claimed 3/50, while Robinson finished with 3/29 as England's pacers completed a comprehensive victory before the tea interval.Pakistan's total of 135 is among their lowest scores in England since 2000, with only their scores of 72, 74 and 80 in 2010, and 119 in 2006 lower during that period. It was also only the second time England's pace bowlers had taken all 20 Pakistan wickets in a Test, the previous instance coming at Lord's in 2001.
Article Summary: England beat Pakistan by an innings and 103 runs in the first Test at Headingley. Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue shared all 10 wickets, claiming five apiece as Pakistan slipped from 117/3 to 171 all out. Harry Brook narrowly missed out on a century, scoring 91 off 93 balls. Jordan Cox contributed a fluent 73.

Article Title: 16 years, no 50-plus stand: Pakistan's opening woes continue in England

Pakistan's struggle to produce a strong opening partnership in England has now lasted 16 years. They have not had a 50-plus opening stand in their last 27 Test innings in England. Their last opening partnership of 50 or more came in 2010.The same problem returned in the first Test against England at Headingley in Leeds.Pakistan could not get a good start in either innings.In the first innings, Azan Awais was dismissed for a duck by Ollie Robinson off the very first ball of the three-match series.Robinson got one to come back sharply from around the wicket and trapped Awais. Imam-ul-Haq was dismissed for a duck by Jofra Archer, leaving Pakistan without another 50-plus opening stand.Pakistan did manage to recover in their first innings after the early damage.Following a two-hour rain delay, Imam-ul-Haq and Abdullah Shafique put together a 91-run stand for the third wicket. Imam scored 42, while Shafique made 61.However, Pakistan could not build on that partnership.They collapsed from 117-3 to 171 all out.England's pace attack then finished the job, with Ollie Robinson taking 5-51 and Josh Tongue claiming 5-46.England made an impressive start to the post-Bazball era as their bowlers dominated Pakistan on the opening day.After bowling Pakistan out for 171, England reached 112-2 at stumps and were only 59 runs behind.Joe Root, starting his second stint as England captain after Ben Stokes' retirement, was unbeaten on 37. Article Title: Pakistan's Ali Usman becomes first visiting left-arm spinner in 16 years to achieve this feat in England

He dismissed Jordan Cox for 73, Harry Brook for 91, Dan Lawrence for 51, Gus Atkinson for 3 and Ollie Robinson for a duck.Brook's 91 was the highest score for England, while Cox and Lawrence also scored half-centuries.England's lower order made an important contribution after the hosts started the day on 366-8. India spin bowling coach Sairaj Bahutule has backed Kuldeep Yadav after his quiet outing in the first Test against Sri Lanka, saying the left-arm wrist spinner remains an important part of the team's plans ahead of the second Test in Colombo.Kuldeep picked up just one wicket in 25 overs across both innings in Galle, while Ravindra Jadeja and Manav Suthar shared 14 wickets between them.Bahutule said Kuldeep's role in Galle was different because of the conditions and the nature of the Kookaburra ball."He's been bowling extremely well. It's just the situation which arose in Galle, he had to play a different role. For me, he has always been a match-winner and he definitely is in the scheme of things," Bahutule told reporters at the Sinhalese Sports Club in Colombo.He explained that wrist spinners face a bigger challenge once the Kookaburra ball becomes soft, while finger spinners can adjust their pace and grip more easily."All the spinners are struggling with the soft ball. But for finger spinners (left-arm or off-spinners), it becomes easier. For a leg-spinner, it is that much harder because of the softness of the ball, the seam just goes down."Finger spinners, you can manipulate the fingers and bowl with the speeds you want to bowl.It is a tough proposition for a (wrist) spinner."So, I don't think one game decides on the way he is performing and the way he is approaching. So, that's all he had to adapt to and he tried his best to adapt to that role."Bahutule said Kuldeep had to keep changing his pace and trajectory as the pitch slowed down during the Test."We had to see how the trajectory or the speeds work in every session. As the days went by and as there was a demand for different types of speeds and different types of trajectories, he definitely was making an effort to bowl that."I think he was playing his role. Article Title: 'Pass on the weed': Ex-India cricketer mocks AB de Villiers over Virat Kohli- Sachin Tendulkar take

Former India fast bowler Dodda Ganesh has taken a cheeky dig at South African great AB de Villiers after he rated Virat Kohli ahead of Sachin Tendulkar in overseas Test conditions.De Villiers recently sparked a debate by saying Kohli was a stronger batter than Tendulkar in seam-friendly and bouncy conditions. While praising Tendulkar for showing that a subcontinent batter could succeed overseas, the former South Africa batter felt Kohli took that legacy forward and raised the bar."I think of someone like Sachin Tendulkar way back, who started that trend for India. Yet, he wasn't as strong as someone like Virat Kohli, who was even better. But Sachin was the first guy to show that as a subcontinent batter, you can do well in bouncy and seaming conditions. Virat took that forward and raised the bar," he said.Ganesh did not agree with the assessment and responded to the comments on X with a cheeky one-liner."Pass on the weed, brother," he wrote.De Villiers and Kohli share a close friendship, which perhaps explains the former South Africa batter's assessment. However, Tendulkar's overseas Test numbers provide a strong counterpoint.Tendulkar scored 8,705 runs in 106 overseas Tests at an average of 54.7, including 29 centuries.Kohli has 4,894 runs in 68 overseas Tests at an average of 41.51.While Kohli has several remarkable Test achievements to his name, Tendulkar's overall record remains difficult to overlook. In every country except the West Indies, Tendulkar has a better Test record than Kohli, although the former's considerably longer career is an important factor.Tendulkar's longevity was particularly evident towards the end of his career. In the final four years of his career, he scored 2,951 runs, eight centuries and 14 fifties in 29 Tests. Kohli, in comparison, managed 1,912 runs in 36 Tests between 2020 and 2025.Kohli certainly has achievements that Tendulkar did not. He scored four centuries in the 2014-15 Border-Gavaskar Trophy, led India to their first Test series win in Australia and produced two outstanding calendar years, scoring 1,215 runs in 2016 and 1,322 in 2018. He also scored 650-plus runs in a Test series on two occasions.But Tendulkar's late-career resurgence was extraordinary. In 2010, aged 37, he scored more than 1,500 runs in 14 Tests, including seven centuries. He scored 213 runs against South Africa, 390 against Sri Lanka and 403 against Australia that year.He then continued that form into 2011, scoring 326 runs in three Tests in South Africa and completing his 50th and 51st Test centuries.Kohli's Test legacy, meanwhile, extends beyond his batting numbers. As captain, he played a major role in transforming India's approach to Test cricket and led the team to a historic series win in Australia.His peak years remain among the finest by an Indian batter. In 2018, he scored 697 runs in England, including three centuries, and also became the first Indian to score four double-centuries in a calendar year.There is little debate over Kohli's standing in white-ball cricket, where his record puts him among the very best. But when the comparison is specifically about Test cricket, de Villiers' assessment is certain to remain contentious.
Article Summary: Former India fast bowler Dodda Ganesh takes a cheeky dig at AB de Villiers. De Villiers recently rated Virat Kohli ahead of Sachin Tendulkar in overseas Test conditions. Kohli has 4,894 runs in 68 overseas Tests at an average of 41.51.

Article Title: Rajasthan stuck in 2012, Manipur in 2023: How actively are states with CWG medals promoting sports?
Article Text:
Are sports bodies of Indian states promoting the game properly?

Manipur still talking about 2023

Rajasthan: 14 years and counting

The ones somewhere in the middle

Does it matter so much?

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Social media presence Local sports events Government funding 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Somewhere on a muddy school field in Haryana right now, a teenager is perhaps drilling the same throwing technique over and over, just as she had watched on television just days ago. Her sole aim is to pull off the one like Sharmila Dhankar, India's Commonwealth Games shot put gold medallist.Before the 2026 CWG campaign, she, like many of us, had almost certainly never heard the name. And it's not because Dhankar had not won anything before the Glasgow Games; she had, a gold medal in the Women's Shot Put F57 event at the 2026 Fazza International Para Athletics Championship, but because one of the primary institutions whose entire job was to carry that story back from the medal podium to villages and training grounds across the state has, for all practical purposes, gone quiet.That's the part of this story that rarely gets told. India walked away from Glasgow with 39 medals, and for a week, the athletes who won them were everywhere, garlanded at airports, seated beside ministers, their faces on the evening news. But medals don't build the next generation of athletes by themselves. Somebody has to keep telling their stories, long after the felicitation photo is filed away, to the kid training in a dusty school ground who needs proof that this path actually leads somewhere.We wanted to know which state sports departments are still doing their job of promoting the sports and their grassroots on their social media platforms, and which ones seem to have simply logged off. So we scrolled through the timelines ourselves. Here's what we found.No state produced more glory in Glasgow than Haryana. Eleven medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze, spanning boxing, wrestling, athletics, and para sport, headlined by a Neeraj Chopra silver that will be replayed on sports channels for years.Alongside him were names most of India still had little knowledge of. The likes of Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Sachin Siwach, and Ankush Panghal, all of whom trained in government facilities, under government schemes, and who'd probably appreciate their own state department cheering as loudly for them as it does for its concert lineups.Because that's the thing. The Sports Department, Government of Haryana's X account has posted exactly once in all of 2026, and it's a flyer for the music acts playing at the Chief Minister's Cup.Facebook and Instagram follow a similar rhythm with a short cluster of posts around that February event, and then not much else.Eleven medals, and not one dedicated post to show for it. Somewhere in Rohtak or Bhiwani, a young pugilist training in Priya Ghanghas's discipline would probably just like a little proof that someone up top is paying attention.Manipur's page has an odd time-capsule quality to it. This is the state that gave India Mirabai Chanu, one of the country's most beloved Olympic medalists, and this Commonwealth Games alone produced four medalists from Manipur, Chanu's gold among them, alongside Rishikanta Singh, Bindyarani Devi, and Jadumani Singh.And yet the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports' X account hasn't posted since October 2023, a "Run for Unity" event, frozen well before any of this year's medals happened.Although the Facebook page has had a few sporadic posts here and there this year, its Instagram account has managed just two posts since January. It’s the kind of gap that makes you wonder if someone simply forgot the login details somewhere along the way.If there's one number in this whole exercise worth sitting with, it's this: the official Sports Department, Government of Rajasthan hasn't posted on Facebook since April 14, 2012.Fourteen years, through Arundhati Choudhary's Commonwealth gold and everything else that's happened in Rajasthan sport since.Its X account's last original post predates a retweet from March 2021, and there's no Instagram at all. A parallel handle, the Rajasthan State Sports Council, exists across all three platforms and is barely livelier.Somewhere behind Choudhary's medal is a genuinely good story, but it just hasn't found a home on the one page built to tell it.Gulveer Singh managed both a silver and a bronze for Uttar Pradesh this Games, a rare double that would make a great centrepiece for the state's sporting year. Instead, across two separate official handles on three platforms, Uttar Pradesh Sports has produced little beyond reposts, while its sister account, Sports Directorate, Govt of Uttar Pradesh, hasn't posted at all in 2026.Delhi Government, for its part, doesn't run a dedicated sports account at all on any of the popular social media platforms, so gold medalist Harsh Singh and bronze medalist Tejaswin Shankar, both representing India's capital, don't really have an institutional cheerleader online, their wins quietly absorbed into the general churn of city government updates. Both athletes are, in effect, doing their own promotional legwork.Set against all that quiet, Tamil Nadu feels like a different sport altogether. Its Sports Tamil Nadu handles post multiple times a day, celebrating not just its own three medalists, Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu, Muthupandi Raja, but athletes from other states too, weaving in government scheme updates without it ever reading like bureaucracy.Every medallist got a dedicated post. Somewhere in Tamil Nadu, a kid training in long jump or wrestling doesn't have to wonder whether the sport leads anywhere. The state tells them, publicly, almost daily.Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka's Facebook and Instagram pages, Assam, Bihar, and Tripura all follow a version of that same habit, active, consistent, generous with attention toward athletes nobody outside their district would otherwise know existed.Kerala doesn't run a separate sports handle on X but keeps its Facebook and Instagram genuinely lively, making sure Murali Sreeshankar and Mohammed Basil's silvers got their due.Andhra Pradesh mirrors that same rhythm across all three platforms.Not every state falls neatly into being inactive or staying proactive. Punjab's account managed just two posts on X all year, New Year's and Republic Day, though its Facebook and Instagram carry a bit more life around coaching and departmental meetings, even if athletes rarely get top billing.Uttarakhand was genuinely active last year before cooling off in 2026, leaning more toward government scheme announcements on Facebook, though its Instagram at least carried two posts around the Games.Maharashtra has dedicated posts up for both Sarvesh Kushare and Dilip Gavit, with Instagram staying fairly regular, enough effort to stay out of the quiet column.Karnataka's X account hasn't posted since March 2024, around an unrelated cultural-team event, even though its Facebook and Instagram have stayed warm and active toward its CWG medalists.It is worth asking why this actually matters, beyond good manners. Well, a state sports department's social media feed isn't just a courtesy board for congratulations; it's one of the cheapest, most direct tools available to build the next generation of athletes.A youngster in a small town is far more likely to pick up a javelin because they saw a state government post celebrating someone from their own district. Even when it comes to promoting any government policy, social media can be as effective.Visibility drives aspiration. There's a funding logic too. Sponsors, corporates, and even state finance departments allocate resources partly based on visible public interest, and a well-run social account is often the easiest evidence a sport has that interest.ALSO READ: Anahat Singh: What is in the name? A word from Guru Nanak's prayer, now India's squash sensation Silence, on the other hand, sends the message that grassroots sport isn't a priority worth the effort of a single post, even when the state has just produced a medallist on the world stage.It is worth it because sometimes, the first step towards building a sporting culture is simply showing people that their achievements are being seen.
Article Summary: India won 39 medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Haryana produced 11 medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze. But the state sports department has posted just once in all of 2026. What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Government funding or social media presence? Share your view.

Article Title: ‘That video was not ordinary’: PM Modi praises Lovlina for objecting to distorted India map - Watch
Article Text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi shares a light moment with boxer Lovlina Borgohain. (PTI Photo)

‘That video was not ordinary’

Mirabai opens up about four difficult years

Narender's joke leaves Modi laughing

NEW DELHI: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain's decision to object to a distorted Indian map during the Commonwealth Games earned special appreciation from Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time.Lovlina, who won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow, was among India's medal winners who interacted with Modi at his residence on Sunday. The meeting, attended by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha, saw athletes recount their experiences from the Games in an informal and emotional setting.In a little over 10-minute video of the interaction shared by the Prime Minister's Office on Monday, Modi brought up Lovlina's confrontation with a restaurant in Glasgow after she noticed a distorted Indian map.“Kya hua wo restaurant waale se jhagda kar rahi thi? (What happened, you were fighting with that restaurant guy?)” Modi asked.Lovlina laughed before explaining why she intervened.“We had such a good performance and it was the last day of the Games. It was a happy occasion sir, we were celebrating and I didn't like it when I saw the distorted map. I politely told them and they have made the changes also,” she explained.Modi applauded the boxer for noticing the issue despite being in the middle of celebrations after her medal-winning campaign.“To be able to recognise the significance of that map at a time when you were celebrating and the Games were over, I can tell you truthfully, that video was not ordinary. It will be remembered by people for a very long time,” he told the Tokyo Olympics bronze medallist.India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.The interaction also provided an emotional window into Mirabai Chanu's journey to her gold medal in the women's 48kg category. The weightlifter produced a Games-record lift of 190kg, but her triumph came after four difficult years following her one-kilogram miss at the Paris Olympics. Modi asked Mirabai about the tears she shed on the podium and even fed her a laddu during their interaction.“Itne aansu tapak rahe the (So many tears were rolling down),” Modi remarked.Mirabai explained that the tears represented years of accumulated emotions.“I was very happy and emotional at that moment. I was crying because I missed a medal in the Paris Olympics by one kilogram. I have faced a lot in these last four years. I was battling injuries and some family problems too.“There were a lot of things. So, these four years were very tough for me. And when I stood on the podium, our flag went up and the anthem played, it was hard to stop myself,” she said.The meeting also had its lighter moments. Boxer Narender Berwal, who won silver in the +90kg category, recalled a funny exchange with a Pakistani boxer after beating him at the 2015 World Military Games.“During the 2015 World Military Games, I had a bout with a Pakistani boxer. I won it but when we were together in the medical room for treatment to our niggles, he said to me 'Bhaijan aapka naam Narender hai, aapke coach ka naam Narender hai, aapke Pradhan Mantri ka naam Narender hai, mujhe Narender naam se nafrat ho gayi hai.' (Brother, you, your coach and your PM are all named Narender. I hate this name now),” he recalled, drawing laughter from Modi.The Prime Minister also underlined the broader significance of the athletes' achievements, saying their medals were helping inspire a new generation.“I have been in this house for 12-13 years now and if there is one group that I have met regularly here, it is the athletes because of your efforts to win medals for India and your tradition of scaling new heights.“Far more than our push to promote sports in schools, it is your medals that inspire people,” Modi said.
Article Summary: Lovlina Borgohain won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow. Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time. India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.

Article Title: ‘From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping’: PM Modi’s heartfelt message to CWG heroes - Watch
Article Text:
PM Narendra Modi interacted with India's CWG 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday. (Pic credit: PM Modi's X post)

NEW DELHI: “From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping.”Prime Minister Narendra Modi had an emotional message for Mirabai Chanu as he interacted with India's Commonwealth Games 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday, reflecting on the sacrifices behind the country's successful campaign in Glasgow.Modi hosted the medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg and heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys at the Games. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze, finishing fourth in the overall standings.During one of the conversations, Modi recalled the emotional scenes surrounding Mirabai's gold-medal triumph.“Tears were falling from you. I feel as if from every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping,” Modi told the Olympic silver medallist.Mirabai, who won gold in Glasgow, opened up about the difficult journey that preceded her Commonwealth Games triumph, including the disappointment of the Paris Olympics.“I was very happy, and emotional too. That day the happiness was greater and I cried because at the Paris Olympics, I lost a medal by 1 kg. In a player’s life what all we have to face. So within these 4 years, how much and what all I had faced, every time injuries were going on and all that was happening.So with great difficulty I had faced these 4 years. So when all that happened, on the podium when I stood, sir, and when our flag goes up and our national anthem plays, sir, we cannot stop, sir, tears come out on their own,” she said.Modi responded by highlighting the wider impact of the athletes' achievements.“This is very good. It is not as if this achievement of yours is considered only your achievement; your victory becomes a very big inspiration for the coming generations.”The informal interaction also saw athletes share lighter and deeply personal moments from their Glasgow campaigns.Modi reminded para shot put gold medallist Sharmila Dhankar of a promise she had made earlier.“You made a promise. Last time, yours, both daughters will become players,” Modi said with a smile.Dhankar replied: “Haanji, right now they are young in age. In the next Commonwealth, one family will bring 3 medals.”Men's 100m T47 gold medallist Dilip Gavit, meanwhile, spoke about dedicating his performance to his guru.“When I was running, when my event was on 29th (July), that day was Guru Purnima, so that day I gave a gift to my guru,” he was heard saying in the video.In another video posted by Modi, gold medallist boxer Sakshi Chaudhary introduced herself and the contingent.“Hello friends! This is Sakshi Chaudhary. Today, our honourable Prime Minister has invited us, the Commonwealth Games medalists, and we feel very proud. We are extremely happy to have met him; he is very humble. Sir, would you like to say something?” she said.Modi replied with a message that summed up his interaction with the athletes: “Jo khelega, woh khilega” (The one who plays, will blossom). “Always cheer for Bharat.”India's fourth-place finish came despite a significantly smaller contingent and a reduced sporting programme compared to Birmingham 2022. India sent 122 athletes to Glasgow, compared to 210 in Birmingham, while 30 of its 61 medals in 2022 came in sports that were not part of the Glasgow programme.Despite those limitations, India retained its fourth-place position and improved its medal conversion rate, with 38 athletes returning home with medals. Long-distance runner Gulveer Singh was the only Indian athlete to win two medals.The Glasgow Games concluded after 11 days, with Scotland handing over the Commonwealth Games flag and ceremonial baton to India ahead of the 2030 edition in Ahmedabad.The symbols were handed to Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra, Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha and Gujarat Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi during the closing ceremony.Ahmedabad will become only the second Indian city to host the Commonwealth Games after New Delhi staged the 2010 edition.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi hosted medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg. Modi heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze.

Article Title: From hospital bed to CWG gold: How Jaismine Lamboria fought the odds in Glasgow
Article Text:
India's Jaismine Lamboria celebrates after winning the women's 57kg boxing final. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Just weeks before stepping into the ring at the Commonwealth Games, Jaismine Lamboria wasn’t thinking about medals. She was searching for answers. The recurring fever had refused to go away.Multiple medical tests showed nothing unusual and the Indian boxer tried to push through, managing the symptoms with paracetamol. When the illness persisted, she was admitted to a hospital in Mohali. Doctors finally diagnosed a bacterial infection, putting her on an intensive 14-day course of medication. For an athlete preparing for one of the biggest competitions of the year, it could easily have been the end of the campaign.Instead, it became the beginning of one of the most remarkable comebacks of her career. “I was avoiding further medical tests because the initial reports were coming back normal. We didn’t know what exactly had to be treated. Finally, after I was admitted, they detected a bacterial infection and I was on medication for 14 days,” the 57kg boxer said.When she was discharged, the clock was already ticking. Barely three weeks remained before the Games.“I started training only on July 1. Initially it was just warm-up, walking and stretching. I had very little time, so we had to be patient.”The physical recovery was only one part of the challenge. During those uncertain weeks, sports psychologist Priya Vrinda became a constant source of support, ensuring the illness didn’t break her confidence.“When I was sick, I was already connected with Priya Vrinda ma’am. She kept me mentally strong and never allowed me to go down,” Jaismine said. That resilience was evident when she returned to competition. Jaismine boxed with maturity, tactical discipline and composure to upgrade the Commonwealth bronze she had won four years ago into gold in the 57kg.One of Jaismine’s biggest assets inside the ring has been her reach in her category. While every opponent may not be shorter — Jaismine stands five feet seven inches in her socks — she believes her physical advantage has become an important weapon thanks to careful coaching. “My coaches taught me how to use my reach properly. It definitely gives me an advantage in many bouts.”
Article Summary: Jaismine Lamboria won gold in the women's 57kg boxing at the Commonwealth Games. The Indian boxer had been suffering from a recurring fever. Doctors diagnosed a bacterial infection and put her on a 14-day course of medication. Jaismine credits her coach Priya Vrinda with helping her recover.

Article Title: How Jadumani Singh's risky weight change nearly derailed his CWG dream before winning Glasgow silver
Article Text:
India's Jadumani Singh Mandengbam (PTI Photo)

A bold gamble after the 50kg category disappeared

The selection maze before Glasgow

Jadumani Si​ngh's Road to CWG Silver (AI-generated Infographic)

The Sports Ministry hurdle

Jadumani Singh Mandengbam (PTI Photo)

Why the gold slipped away

File Pic: L Sarita Devi (PTI Photo)

Olympic gold remains the ultimate dream

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: When Indian pugilist Jadumani Singh Mandengbam stepped onto the podium to receive the men's 55kg silver medal at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, it marked the culmination of a journey that had almost ended before it had even begun.The 22-year-old Manipuri boxer was one of India's standout performers, winning four consecutive unanimous 5-0 verdicts to storm into the bantamweight final before settling for silver against Australia's Jye Dixon. His medal also formed part of India's historic boxing campaign, which yielded seven golds and three silvers, making the country the No. 1 boxing nation at the Games for the first time.Yet, behind that success lay months of uncertainty, selection hurdles and a weight-category gamble that nearly cost him a place on the flight to Scotland.Speaking exclusively to TimesofIndia.com, former world champion and Jadumani's mentor, Laishram Sarita Devi, recounted how the young boxer refused to abandon his Olympic dream even when every obstacle seemed stacked against him.Jadumani had built his reputation in the 50kg category, winning medals at World Boxing Cups before learning that the division would no longer feature in the Commonwealth Games, Asian Games or Olympic programme.Rather than remain in a non-Olympic category, he decided to move up to 55kg — a division already occupied by some of India's biggest names."He continued to consult with me. Whenever he had to make a big decision, he called up and consulted with me — like increasing his weight category," Sarita told TimesofIndia.com."After he won a World Cup medal in 50kg, he got to know that the weight category is no longer in the CWG, Asian Games and Olympics. He wanted to move to 55kg."The decision immediately brought fresh challenges."Army had their No. 1 boxer in the 55kg category in Pune, who is Services' No. 1 boxer. And the weight category also has Amit Panghal — Olympian and Asian champion. He said he wanted to move up the weight to compete at CWG, Asian Games etc, but was discouraged by hearing questions like whether he would be able to compete at that level, which created a doubt in him," she said.Sarita, however, wanted only one answer: "We sat down and I asked him, 'Are you confident about the decision?' He said he was, so I told him to move up the category."The decision created another problem.Without competing in the National Championships, Jadumani could not enter the national coaching camp. But because he belonged to the Army Sports Institute, Services already had its designated 55kg representative. Attempts to let him represent Manipur also failed."We tried to make him compete for the state of Manipur, but we didn't get an NOC because he is with the Army," Sarita said.Relief finally arrived through a Boxing Federation of India (BFI) policy that granted direct entries to the National Championships for World Boxing Cup medallists. The move was aimed at rewarding elite international performers and ensuring they were not blocked by the usual domestic qualification pathways.The decision allowed Jadumani to compete directly in the 55kg draw despite the institutional overlap, resulting in multiple squad members — Pawan Bartwal, Jadumani Singh and Amit Panghal — finding themselves in the same weight-category draw.Sarita said her ward grabbed the opportunity with both hands."He then got a chance to compete in 55kg in the Nationals. Due to his effort, he won against the Services No.1, Olympians etc to be named Best Boxer in the Nationals. After that he got the chance to be part of the India camp," she said.He then cleared the final selection trials, which included physical assessments alongside ring performances."He participated in the final trial for the CWG and Asian Games — which had many aspects like strength and endurance tests before fighting in the ring. He won all of it to get selected for the CWG and was really happy and started training hard," she added.Just when Glasgow appeared certain, another setback emerged.Because Jadumani had only recently moved into 55kg, he did not possess the Asian ranking required under the Sports Ministry's eligibility criteria for Commonwealth Games selection."He got an explanation mail from the Sports Ministry, which put him in immense tension ahead of the Games," Sarita recalled.Under the ministry's guidelines, boxers were expected to be ranked among Asia's top eight in their respective categories."He was ranked No. 2 in 50kg, but he lacked a ranking in the new 55kg category. He had only competed in one Asian Championship in the new weight category before the trials for CWG and, being new to the category, lost in the quarterfinals," she said.That led to fresh doubts over his selection."He was disheartened when questions were raised whether he was a medal prospect because he was not in the rankings prescribed by the ministry. He called me and said the coaches were saying he may or may not be on the flight to the CWG because of this letter from the ministry," she recalled.The uncertainty only ended after BFI submitted a detailed explanation to the ministry, outlining Jadumani's circumstances following his weight-category switch."BFI replied to the ministry properly, explaining everything and after a lot of effort his ticket to Glasgow was approved. What I like about him is that he is the kind of person who doesn't give up and has a very strong will power," she said.Jadumani eventually reached the final after four demanding contests, each won by an identical 5-0 margin. But Sarita believes the scheduling ultimately worked against him."Jadumani's four bouts were very tough. He played all out in all the bouts till the semifinals as he got proper rest and recovery time. Since the gold medal opponent got a bye earlier, he had fewer bouts than Jadumani," she explained.The semifinal-final turnaround, she felt, proved decisive. There was a one-day gap after every bout until the semifinals, but there was no gap between the semifinal and final in Glasgow."Jadumani fought his semifinal in the evening and got the final bout the next morning only, so he did not get much time for recovery. If it was in the evening, he could have fought better. When he entered the ring for the final, I saw his face and body language sitting here and realised he had not had enough recovery," she said.The experience, she believes, underlines the growing importance of sports science."In such situations, we should look for how we can enhance or speed up the recovery process through sports science. We should discuss it to make sure our boxers can give 100 per cent every time they enter the ring," she added.Sarita first noticed Jadumani as a youngster competing in a local tournament."When I saw Jadumani for the first time, it was a tournament for young boys. His movement was really pleasing and I thought he could become a good boxer in the future. I identified him at that time only and gave him Rs 500 because I was very pleased with his performance," she recalled."Jadumani did not start with me from the grassroots. He learnt his basics from another academy. He came to my academy when he was preparing to enrol in the Army Sports Institute in Pune. At that time, I did not have any infrastructure and was coaching from a makeshift setup. And then Covid happened, we had to train in a very isolated small makeshift place,” she added.Years later, after training together through difficult Covid-19 conditions and watching him overcome one hurdle after another, Sarita believes Glasgow is only the beginning."We missed gold at the CWG, but we will work hard to get gold at the Asian Games for sure," she said.The bigger ambition, however, stretches far beyond continental success."His first and primary target remains Olympic gold. Commonwealth Games and Asian Games are the stepping stones in that journey. He will try to win India's first Olympic gold medal in boxing," Sarita concluded.
Article Summary: Jadumani Singh Mandengbam won silver at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. The 22-year-old Manipuri boxer won four consecutive unanimous 5-0 verdicts to storm into the bantamweight final before settling for silver against Australia's Jye Dixon. His medal also formed part of India's historic boxing campaign, which yielded seven golds and three silvers, making the country the No. 1 boxing nation at the Games.

Article Title: Days after historic CWG gold, Dilip Gavit leaves without meeting Raj Thackeray after two-hour wait
Article Text:

Just days after scripting history for Indian para athletics at the Commonwealth Games, gold medallist Dilip Gavit found himself making headlines for a very different reason. The 23-year-old sprinter, who became India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medallist in the men's 100m T47 event, waited for nearly two hours to meet Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray in Nashik on Thursday before leaving without the meeting taking place.According to Gavit's coach quoted by PTI, Vaijanath Kale, the para-athlete had been invited to meet Thackeray during the MNS chief's visit to Nashik.
